summary: Designing processes with flowcharts — standard symbols, sequence, selection and loops, and turning a flowchart into pseudocode.

blocks.content: A diagram that shows the **sequence of steps and decisions** in a process or algorithm using standard symbols joined by arrows.

blocks.title: Flowchart symbols
rows: A Yes/No question: `price < 1000?` — two labelled exits

blocks.content:
flowchart TD
  A([START]) --> B[/INPUT price/]
  B --> C{price < 1000?}
  C -- Yes --> D[selling ← price × 1.3]
  C -- No --> E[selling ← price × 1.15]
  D --> F[/OUTPUT selling/]
  E --> F
  F --> G([STOP])
blocks.caption: Selling price: +30% if the price is under 1000, otherwise +15%

blocks.content:
flowchart TD
  A([START]) --> B[profit ← 0]
  B --> C[/INPUT code/]
  C --> D{code = 'END'?}
  D -- Yes --> H[/OUTPUT profit/]
  H --> I([STOP])
  D -- No --> E[/INPUT price, selling/]
  E --> F[profit ← profit + selling − price]
  F --> C
blocks.caption: Total profit of all products sold in a day (condition-controlled loop)

blocks.content:
profit ← 0
INPUT code
WHILE code <> "END" DO
    INPUT price, selling
    profit ← profit + (selling - price)
    INPUT code
ENDWHILE
OUTPUT profit
blocks.caption: The same loop as pseudocode

blocks.title: Loop types
rows: Runs a fixed number of times
**After** each pass — runs at least once

blocks.content: Mark schemes for flowcharts usually award separate marks for: correct **input**, correct **process/calculation**, correct **decision** with Yes/No labels, a working **loop**, correct **output**, and START/STOP. Label both exits of every decision.
A decision diamond has **exactly one** entry and **two** exits (Yes/No). Never leave a branch that goes nowhere — every path must reach STOP.
